title: Map Work
tagline: Reading, interpreting and marking maps: scale, projection, direction, conventional symbols and the interpretation of topographic sheets.

overview.intro: A map is a simplified, scaled representation of part of the Earth’s surface, and the skill being examined is the ability to read information from one and to record information on one accurately. This unit covers the elements of a map, the common methods of representing scale and their advantages, the main types of map projection and the distortion each introduces, conventional symbols and colour conventions, direction through compass rose and grid, and the interpretation of contour and topographic sheets, including inter-contour distance, gradient and the identification of landforms from contour patterns.

facts.label: Map elements
facts.value: Title, scale, direction, conventional symbols, keys or legend, grid reference and projection.

facts.label: Scale
facts.value: Representative fraction, statement or linear scale; a large scale covers a small area in detail, a small scale covers a large area with less detail.

facts.label: Projection
facts.value: Conical, cylindrical and planar projections each preserve some property and distort others.

facts.label: Contours
facts.value: Lines joining places of equal height; close spacing means steep ground and wide spacing means gentle ground.

learningOutcomes: State the elements of a map and the methods of showing scale.
Explain the main types of projection and what they distort.
Use conventional symbols, colour and grid references.
Interpret contour patterns to identify landforms and slopes.
Calculate gradient and distance from a map scale.

learn.title: Elements of a map and representation of scale

blocks.text: Every usable map carries the same basic elements. The title states what the map shows and where. Scale relates distance on the map to distance on the ground, and it may be expressed as a statement such as one centimetre to a kilometre, a representative fraction such as 1:50,000 where the numerator and denominator are in the same units, or a linear scale drawn as a bar that can be measured directly. Direction is shown by a north arrow or compass rose, and the conventional symbols for roads, railways, water and buildings are explained in a key. A grid provides the reference system by which a point can be located precisely.

blocks.caption: Methods of representing scale
rows: Immediately understood by a general reader
Unit-free, so it works in any system of measurement
A ruled bar marked in km
Can be read directly with a strip of paper, survives enlargement

blocks.text: The relationship between scale and detail runs inversely. A large-scale map such as 1:10,000 covers a small area and shows fine detail including individual buildings. A small-scale map such as 1:1,000,000 covers a vast area and can only show broad features, so detail is sacrificed for extent. Confusing the two is the commonest error in map questions, because a large fraction means a large scale.

items.text: A town plan at 1:10,000 shows individual houses.
items.note: Large scale, small area, high detail.

items.text: A continental map at 1:5,000,000 shows only major rivers and cities.
items.note: Small scale, huge area, low detail.

blocks.text: A projection is the mathematical way of representing the curved surface of the Earth on a flat sheet, and every projection distorts something, because a sphere cannot be flattened without stretching. A conical projection places a cone over the globe and unrolls it, giving accurate shape and scale along the standard parallels, and it is well suited to mid-latitude countries with an east-west extent. A cylindrical projection, such as Mercator’s, wraps a cylinder around the Earth, giving correct direction which made it valuable for navigation, but exaggerating area enormously toward the poles. A planar or azimuthal projection projects from a point, giving correct directions from the centre and being suitable for polar maps.

blocks.caption: Main types of projection
rows: Shape and scale along standard parallels

blocks.text: Colour follows a convention the candidate is expected to know. Blue is used for water in all forms, from sea to river to glacier, though ice may be shown in blue-white. Green denotes vegetation and low land, brown or orange represents relief and contours, black is used for man-made features such as roads, buildings and railways, and red commonly marks main roads and settlement. The same conventions apply to symbols, so a dashed line normally denotes a track or seasonal road and a solid double line a metalled road.

Contours are lines joining points of equal height above sea level, and they allow three-dimensional relief to be read from a flat sheet. Four properties govern their reading: the value of the contour interval stated in the key; the spacing of the lines, which is close where the slope is steep and wide where it is gentle; the shape of the lines, which identifies the landform; and the direction of the gradient, which is always at right angles to the contour and downhill.

blocks.caption: Contour patterns and the landforms they show
rows: Contour lines forming concentric closed loops, higher inward
Closed loops with heights decreasing inward
V shape pointing upstream or uphill
Contours crossing a river at right angles in a V
A valley cut into the surface

blocks.text: Gradient is calculated as the vertical difference in height divided by the horizontal distance between the two points, usually expressed as a percentage or as a ratio. An example: if the height rises from 200 metres to 320 metres over a horizontal distance of 1.2 kilometres, the rise is 120 metres and the gradient is 120 divided by 1,200, which is 0.1, or 10 per cent, or 1 in 10. Inter-contour distance on a map is converted to ground distance by multiplying by the scale factor.

items.text: Contours 4 mm apart at 1:50,000 between 100 m and 150 m.
items.note: Ground distance is 200 m, so the rise of 50 m over 200 m gives a 25 per cent gradient.

items.text: A river valley shown by contours crossing it in sharp V shapes.
items.note: The V points upstream, which is how the direction of flow can be read from the sheet.

blocks.text: A grid of eastings and northings gives a precise location. Eastings are vertical lines numbered from west to east and are read first, while northings are horizontal lines numbered from south to north and are read second, so the four-figure reference 4235 names the square bounded by easting 42, easting 43, northing 35 and northing 36. A six-figure reference subdivides that square to locate a point within it to a hundred metres. Direction is measured from the printed north arrow, and where magnetic declination is shown the difference between grid north, magnetic north and true north must be allowed for in a bearing.

items: Read eastings first, northings second: along the corridor, then up the stairs.
Contour interval is stated in the key and applies to every contour on the sheet.
The grid reference locates a square; the six-figure reference locates a point inside it.
Distance on the map converts to ground distance by the scale, so 4 cm at 1:50,000 is 2 km.
Gradient equals vertical difference divided by horizontal distance.

items.text: A well 4234 3571 shown on a six-figure reference.
items.note: The point lies in the square 4235 35, three tenths across and seven tenths up.

items.text: A bridge marked with the conventional symbol and a height in metres.
items.note: Spot heights supplement contours where precise elevation matters.

keyPoints: A map needs a title, scale, direction, symbols, key, grid and projection.
A representative fraction is unit-free; a linear scale can be read directly.
Large scale means small area with much detail; small scale means large area with little detail.
Conical, cylindrical and planar projections each preserve one property and distort others.
Blue is water, green is vegetation, brown is relief, black is man-made and red is main roads.
Contours join equal heights; close spacing means steep ground.
A V in contours points upstream in a valley and downhill on a spur.
Gradient is vertical difference divided by horizontal distance.
Grid references read eastings first and northings second.
Map distance converts to ground distance by the map scale.
examFocus: Scale conversions must show the multiplication, since the working carries marks.
Contour questions reward naming the pattern before naming the landform.
Gradient answers need the units at every step and the final expression as a percentage or a ratio.

questions.prompt: Contours drawn very close together indicate:
questions.explanation: A large change in height over a short horizontal distance means the ground rises steeply.

options: 1 cm on the map represents 50,000 cm on the ground
1 km on the map represents 50 km on the ground
1 m on the map represents 50 m on the ground
The map is 50,000 times smaller than the ground
questions.answer: 1 cm on the map represents 50,000 cm on the ground
questions.explanation: Both numerator and denominator are in the same unit, so 1 cm equals 50,000 cm, which is 500 m.

questions.prompt: Which projection is most suitable for a country spread mainly east-west in mid-latitudes?
questions.explanation: A cone unrolled across the region gives accurate scale and shape along its standard parallels, which suits an east-west extent in middle latitudes.

questions.prompt: In a grid reference, the correct order of reading is:
questions.explanation: Eastings are read along the corridor first and northings up the stairs second, giving for example 4235 before 3571.

questions.prompt: The difference in height between two successive contour lines is called the contour __________ .
questions.explanation: The interval is stated in the key and applies uniformly to the whole sheet, so every contour can be valued.

questions.prompt: A projection that wraps the globe in a cylinder and preserves direction, making it useful for navigation, is the __________ projection.
questions.explanation: It keeps rhumb lines straight, which aided navigation, but it exaggerates area severely toward the poles.

questions.prompt: State four essential elements of a map.
questions.answer: Four elements are: the title, which states what the map shows and where; the scale, relating map distance to ground distance; direction, shown by a north arrow or compass rose; and the key or legend, which explains the symbols used. A grid for reference and the projection used are also accepted.
questions.explanation: Each element needs a line on what it contributes, since a bare list earns only partial credit.

questions.prompt: Distinguish between a large-scale map and a small-scale map.
questions.answer: A large-scale map has a large representative fraction such as 1:10,000, covers a comparatively small area and shows a high level of detail such as individual buildings and field boundaries. A small-scale map has a small fraction such as 1:1,000,000, covers a very large area and can show only broad features such as major rivers and cities. The relationship is therefore inverse in appearance: the larger the fraction, the larger the scale and the smaller the area covered, and a large-scale map is used for detailed local study while a small-scale map is used for regional or world comparison.
questions.explanation: The apparent paradox of the naming must be handled explicitly, since that is where marks are lost.

questions.prompt: Explain how contours are used to identify landforms and to calculate gradient, with a worked example.
questions.answer: Contours join points of equal height, so the pattern they make identifies the relief. Closely spaced contours mean a steep slope and widely spaced contours a gentle one. Closed concentric loops with heights increasing inward indicate a hill, while loops with heights decreasing inward indicate a depression. In a valley the contours form a V that points upstream, since the valley rises as it goes inland, whereas on a spur the V points downhill as the ridge projects outward. To find the gradient, take the difference in height between two contours and divide it by the horizontal distance between them, converting map distance to ground distance by the scale. For example, if the 100 metre and 150 metre contours are 4 mm apart on a map at 1:50,000, the ground distance is 200 metres, so the gradient is 50 divided by 200, which is 0.25 or 25 per cent, equivalently 1 in 4. The direction of the gradient is always at right angles to the contour and downhill.
questions.explanation: Full marks need the pattern recognition and a complete worked calculation with units at each step.

questions.prompt: A map shows contours at 200 m and 260 m crossing a river with V shapes, a road climbing the slope at a steady gradient, and a settlement at a grid reference. State the direction of river flow, calculate the gradient between the two contours if they are 6 mm apart on a 1:50,000 map, and give a six-figure grid reference method for the settlement.
questions.answer: The V shapes in the contours point upstream, so the river flows in the opposite direction to the point of the V, which is the standard way of reading flow direction from a contour sheet. The height difference between the two contours is 60 metres. On a map at 1:50,000, 6 mm represents 300 metres on the ground, so the gradient is 60 divided by 300, which is 0.2, or 20 per cent, or 1 in 5. For the settlement, locate the four-figure square by reading the eastings first and then the northings, for example 4235 35, and then subdivide that square mentally into tenths along both axes, counting three tenths across and seven tenths up to give the six-figure reference 4233 3573. The answer therefore gives direction, a gradient with units and a reference method, which is what the question asks for in each of its three parts.
questions.explanation: Each of the three parts carries its own marks, and the working must be shown for the gradient and the subdivision described for the reference.
